blocks.text: BUILDINGS CHANGE. EVIDENCE REMAINS.
Cities through their layers.
A city is more than the moment it fell.
Explore a place through its rebuilding, ordinary life and surviving traces. Begin with what was found. Then ask what it can tell us.
01 / THE SECTION & THE EVIDENCE
One place. Several histories.
Choose a city, then a horizon. Selected contexts, not complete histories.
Lachish
Tell ed-Duweir · Judah
Number = selected context · dark earth = destruction context · brighter block = your selection
Composite teaching section. Depth, thickness and architecture are illustrative; the spaces between blocks do not measure time.
LATE EIGHTH CENTURY BCE; ASSOCIATED WITH 701
Level III siege and destruction
The fortified city and siege works belong to a different horizon from the later Level II town.
The archaeological sequence is read alongside the Assyrian campaign record and the named Lachish reliefs. This convergence is stronger than assigning a fire to a conquest by date alone.
The association with Sennacherib’s campaign is well supported. It does not establish every detail of 2 Kings 18–19 through archaeology.
THE FINDS TRAY
Small things. Specific questions.
Illustrative fragment · no inscription reproduced
Relief comparison
BM 124906 shows ramps, siege engines and captives. It was excavated at Nineveh and dates to about 700–692 BCE.
The image commemorates the campaign after the event; it was not found in Lachish’s destruction layer.
The relief depicts people taken away as well as military equipment: destruction also meant displacement.
Lachish: Level III siege and destruction. Evidence is in the record beside the section.
02 / LEARN TO READ A SECTION
The ground is a sequence of actions.
Before asking who lived here, ask how this deposit came to be. Build a small, imaginary excavation and watch a later event reach into older ground.
Teaching model · invented geometry · no depth or time scale
The pit cuts through the burn deposit and floor. Its bottom is physically low but chronologically late. The cut is an event; the material later filling it is another.
A simplified relationship chain, read left to right; real Harris matrices can branch. Edward C. Harris · Principles of Archaeological Stratigraphy ↗ (opens in a new tab)
03 / FROM SEQUENCE TO DATE
Dates are arguments made from evidence.
A deposit’s position, its contents and its formation history work together. No one method answers every question.
EVIDENCE CLOSE UP / JERICHO
A laboratory date is not a calendar year.

These six published cereal measurements let us inspect the evidence behind the destruction-date discussion. Each dot is a measurement; its whisker shows the reported laboratory uncertainty, not the duration of a historical event.
The 1995 paper’s calibration and a modern recalibration are different analyses. No new calendar probability curve is implied here.
Six measurements. One context question.
Published cereal measurements; whiskers show ±1σ laboratory uncertainty. BP means radiocarbon years before 1950, not calendar BCE.
Barley · GrN-18539 — 3312 ± 14 BP. This is a measurement of organic material, not a dated inscription naming a conquest.
APPLY THE METHOD / TEST AN INTERPRETATION
You uncover a burned room. What can you say first?
04 / HOW UNDERSTANDING CHANGES
A field built through revision.
Excavation destroys the deposits it records. Plans, notebooks, sample labels and published assemblages let later scholars ask questions the original excavators could not.
From a monument to its relationships
Harris’s work makes the sequence itself an object of analysis. A floor, a cut and a fill need separate records. A visually convincing reconstruction cannot substitute for those relationships.
Old archives, new questions

Kenyon’s preserved Jericho material made later laboratory work possible. Renewed Italian–Palestinian work also brings older trenches into dialogue with new excavation and conservation. The site’s history includes homes, water and collective labor, not only the question of conquest.
From a sample to a city

Recent dating projects can sharpen a sequence. They cannot eliminate the need to explain whether the dated material belongs to a construction, a period of use, or later fill. Evidence from one trench also needs justification before it is extended across a city.
Whose city survives in the record?

Palaces and fortifications make rulers visible. Storage jars, cooking vessels, drains and repairs ask about provision, labor and repeated use. A wealthy house is evidence for one part of society; it is not an average household. Excavated space is a sample shaped by access, preservation, earlier digging and modern settlement.

Hebrew and Aramaic inscriptions, Greek and Latin civic records, and Assyrian royal representations have different audiences and purposes. A text’s named place can anchor an identification while its rhetoric still needs interpretation. Jewish and Christian readings may ask theological questions of a biblical passage; an archaeological date does not by itself decide those questions.

British, Palestinian, Italian, Israeli, Greek and international research traditions appear in the sources here. Their publications should be compared through methods and contexts, rather than treated as interchangeable national positions.
Works to read, and what they contribute
The excavation record behind the later sample analysis. To challenge a chronological result, return to the room, phase and deposit assignments, as well as the laboratory measurements.
Access record: Bibliographic reference and use of its phase records checked in Bruins & van der Plicht; full volume not consulted. Link leads to that citing study.

Foundational records against which later excavators test fortification phases. Disagreement about early urban growth depends on which walls, floors and assemblages belong together, not simply on choosing a preferred ruler.
Access record: Bibliographic and historical discussion in the 2019 report consulted; complete earlier excavation volumes not read. Link leads to the later comparison.
A language for recording deposits and surfaces as a sequence of relationships. A matrix expresses what precedes what; it does not supply calendar years.
Access record: Author’s bibliographical and methodological overview consulted; complete book not retrieved.
Re-examines material preserved from Kenyon’s excavation through independent laboratory measurements. Separates short-lived cereals from wood and laboratory precision from calendar uncertainty.
Access record: Full article consulted, especially Table 1, Figures 1–4 and pp. 218–219.
Connects newly excavated architecture with samples from a floor. Helps distinguish dating the use of a building from identifying the political authority responsible for it.
Access record: Full report available; methods, Area CC, Figures 3–4 and results consulted. The political interpretation is the authors’ argument.

Reports 103 determinations from five excavation areas. Connects context assessment, tree-ring comparisons and radiocarbon to a dense urban sequence; precise historical conclusions require reading the models.
Access record: Indexed abstract, significance statement and opening text consulted. Full article retrieval was blocked; supplementary models were not inspected.
An assemblage challenges a simple picture of emptiness between 146 and 44 BCE. This page does not reproduce its object catalogue or estimate the population from it.
Access record: Journal catalogue and indexed passage from p. 62 consulted; full PDF retrieval failed.
Brings renewed excavation, comparison of older trenches and heritage protection together. Palestinian and Italian collaboration widens the story beyond the older European expeditions.
Access record: Institutional catalogue, abstract and indexed introductory page consulted; complete chapter not retrieved.
A route from an overview to excavation records and spatial documentation. The plan and find context are part of the evidence, not merely illustrations.
Access record: Institutional resource description consulted; individual GIS layers and object datasets not downloaded.
The next questions

How securely are samples tied to their deposits? Which buildings share a phase? What survives outside the excavated area? Could a proposed historical identification explain the evidence better than other causes?

Research gaps: the Jerusalem supplementary models, Romano’s full object catalogue, Kenyon’s complete final reports and modern recalibration of the Jericho samples have not been independently reviewed for this expansion. No new calendar probability curve or measured city plan is claimed.
